name: Hassan Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To begin, describe a normal working day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy car and van parts, brake pads, filters, batteries, belts, for a distributor that supplies about six hundred independent garages. I'm in the office by eight, and the first hour is the overnight orders and which parts are about to run out. Then I'm on with the brand suppliers about prices and delivery dates. After lunch I walk the warehouse with Dev, the stock manager, and we argue happily about what's moving. I enjoy it. What I don't enjoy is the constant pressure from electric cars, since fewer moving parts means fewer parts to sell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say it's a handy bit of software and no more. To friends I'd say the hype has been loud and the real change is small. Online I'd stay quiet, I'm not one for arguments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel pretty calm. Buying parts depends on knowing which garages need what, and that's built on years of phone calls. The thing I do worry about is electric cars, which shrink the parts market slowly, but that's already happening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on the same, keep using the forecasting tool now and then, and keep an eye on the market. I'd also keep saving a bit each month and maybe look at some electric vehicle parts lines to buy for the future. Nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's a world I understand and where my experience counts. There's the odd wobble about the firm, but nothing I'd lose sleep over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd stay calm. What's the pressure you do carry?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The shift to electric. Fewer brake pads, no exhausts, no oil filters. Our sales in some lines have fallen by about a tenth in three years. If it falls faster, the firm trims, and I'm paid more than most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change anything about how you work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd run a trial of one of the forecasting tools on a single line, say filters, and compare it with my own estimate for three months. If it beats me, I'd use it. If not, not.

say: At work I'd call it **handy software** and no more.
To friends I'd say the hype is loud and the **real change is small**.
think: Buying rests on **years of phone calls**, so I feel calm about my job.
My real pressure is **electric cars** shrinking the parts market slowly.
do: Keep using the **forecasting tool** now and then.
Look at **electric vehicle** parts lines for the future.
feel: **Calm**, in a world where experience still counts.
S0.quote: Buying parts depends on knowing which garages need what, and that's built on years of phone calls.
fieldNote: He is **calm** because his knowledge is relational, and the pressure he names is the slow shift to electric cars.
He **tests tools** against his own judgement, a steady, proof-first habit.

steps.text: Trial a forecasting tool on filters against my own estimate
Add a bit to monthly savings
Look at buying electric-vehicle parts lines for the future

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the next picture, called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should wait for proof and not rush. At work I'd ask for pilots on small lines and for staff to be told the plan. To friends I'd say it's change we have to manage, not fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm a bit uneasy. A lot of my work is thinking: planning orders, checking prices, matching supplier terms. The tools can do these. I think my job is safe for a while, but my team of three may shrink.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the tools properly, starting with the order-planning one. I'd ask to be the lead on rolling them out, so I shape how the team uses them. And I'd keep building relationships with the brand suppliers, which a tool doesn't have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's not fear for myself yet. It's looking at Dev and the buying assistants and wondering who's next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of your tasks does the card put at risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first draft of every order, and price checks across suppliers. I'd say within three years most of those are automatic. What stays is the negotiation and the oddball situations.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would your team change over those years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd guess one of three goes, probably by not replacing someone. We'd all say it's natural wastage, which means no one is fired but the work gets heavier for everyone. I'd try to push for retraining so that people move into supplier management.

say: I'd say we should **wait for proof** and run pilots on small lines.
I'd say it's change to **manage**, not fear.
think: A lot of my work is **thinking work**: planning orders and checking prices.
My job looks safe for a while, but my **team may shrink**.
do: Ask to **lead** the rollout so I shape it.
feel: **Uneasy**, wondering who's next in the team.
S1.quote: We'd all say it's natural wastage, which means no one is fired but the work gets heavier for everyone.
fieldNote: He is **steady**, choosing to lead the rollout so he shapes it rather than reacting.
His worry is **for colleagues**, and he expects change through natural wastage rather than layoffs.

steps.text: Learn the order-planning tool and lead its rollout in my team
Keep building relationships with brand suppliers
Push for retraining so people can move into supplier management

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the next picture, called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a lot and that nobody knows what to do. I'd call for the government and companies to set out plans. At work I'd say we need to talk openly, not hide it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd say my job is likely gone by 2028. Buying is thinking work, and AI does all of it. The robots three years later hit the warehouse, so Dev's team too. There's no part of the firm that would be safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd cut out unnecessary spending and pay off what we can. I'd ask the firm about early retirement or a payout. I'd start looking at advisory work for small garages and at jobs outside buying. And I'd learn the AI tools better, because it's better to be someone who can use them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd have a plan, so I'm not panicking, but I'd have a lump in the stomach. It's the speed, I'm not used to things changing this fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years. What would you do in the first month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Claire straight away. We've always been open. I'd say we have four months, we'd tighten up, and maybe she'd ask for more hours. We'd lean on the kids for ideas, not money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Claire works three days. What would you tell her?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably downsize in a couple of years. Our house is paid down, so we'd have some room. We'd have a smaller life, not a ruined one.

say: I'd say **nobody knows** what to do, so governments and firms should set out plans.
At work I'd say we need to **talk openly**.
think: My job is **likely gone by 2028**, and the robots would hit Dev's warehouse team three years later.
No part of the firm would be **safe**.
do: Cut **unnecessary spending** and pay off what we can.
Ask the firm about **early retirement** or a payout.
Look at **advisory work** for small garages.
feel: **Anxious**, with a lump in the stomach at the speed.
S2.quote: We'd have a smaller life, not a ruined one.
fieldNote: He is **anxious but organised**, with a plan that includes early retirement and advisory work.
The **couple talk openly**, and Claire may take more hours.

steps.text: Cut unnecessary spending and pay off small debts
Ask the firm about early retirement or a payout
Find advisory work for small garages
Learn the AI tools well enough to use them daily

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the next picture, called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to plan if people start now. I'd say to my firm, set up retraining and don't wait. And to friends, we should use the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it's better. I'd be 63 and can plan an exit. It's still anxious, since the end point is the same, but I'd have time to fix the money side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the years to build the savings to six months, pay off the car, and set up some consultancy for garages. I'd learn the tools well, so that I can teach them to small garages. And in year four or five, I'd go part-time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but manageable. It's like a delayed train, you know it's coming and you plan around it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years instead of two. What does that give you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep seeing them, build a few consultancy jobs and tell them what I'm doing. Garages like a familiar voice, and I'm trusted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about the garages you've worked with so long?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the work picked up, great. If not, I'd retire a bit earlier on a smaller pension. I'd rather have a modest plan than none.

say: I'd say five years is **enough to plan** if people start now.
I'd tell my firm to set up **retraining** and not wait.
think: Five years is better, and I'd be **63** with time to plan an exit.
It's still anxious because the **end point** is the same.
do: Build savings to **six months** and pay off the car.
Set up **consultancy** for garages and teach them the tools.
Go **part-time** in year four or five.
feel: **Anxious but manageable**, like a delayed train.
S3.quote: Garages like a familiar voice, and I'm trusted.
fieldNote: He uses the extra time to **turn relationships into consultancy**, a natural next step for a trusted buyer.
His anxiety is **tempered by planning**, in a steady and measured way.

steps.text: Build savings to six months and pay off the car
Set up consultancy for local garages
Learn the tools well enough to teach garages
Go part-time in year four or five

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the next picture, called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should keep an eye on it, and that people should plan. At work I'd suggest that younger staff get proper training. I'd not be alarmed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be 68, long retired, so I'm uneasy for them, not for me. I'd feel I'd had a decent run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work to 62 or 63, retire, and maybe advise a few garages part-time. I'd keep using the tools on my own work and share what I learn with Dev's team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, mostly. It's a calm kind of unease, like hearing weather news for next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is a long runway. Does it feel different?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To build savings early, keep their relationships alive and learn how the tools work. And to not assume the firm will look after them. They need to look out for themselves a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the younger buyers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd also tell them not to be scared. Ten years is a long time to adapt, and the people who start early will be fine.

say: I'd say we should **keep an eye** on it and plan.
I'd suggest younger staff get **proper training**.
think: I'd be **68 and retired**, so I'm uneasy for them, not for me.
I'd feel I'd had a **decent run**.
do: Share what I learn with **Dev's team**.
feel: **Uneasy** in a calm way, like next year's weather news.
S4.quote: Ten years is a long time to adapt, and the people who start early will be fine.
fieldNote: The long runway makes his unease **about others** rather than himself, in a calm, fatherly tone.
He urges young buyers to **start early**, a steady, practical message.

steps.text: Advise a few garages part-time after retiring
Share what I learn about the tools with the warehouse team

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Five or ten years I could plan around, but two years leaves nothing. I'm 58, we have about four months saved, and Claire only works three days at the library. What would help is a clear notice period, a decent redundancy payment, and some kind of help finding work at my age. I'd want my firm to be straight with us.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'd like to see more middle ground in this debate. Most of us aren't for or against it, we just want it to work and not to wreck anyone's life.

headlineQuote: Most of us aren't for or against it, we just want it to work and not to wreck anyone's life.
portrait: **Hassan** is 58, a senior buyer of car and van parts for a distributor serving about six hundred independent garages.
He is **steady and pragmatic**, uses AI tools now and then, and adopts new things once they're proven.
Centrist in outlook, he **blames no side**, wanting the technology to work without wrecking lives.
With about **four months saved** and a partner working three days a week, a sudden job loss would hurt.
He is calm in a quiet world, then grows **anxious** as the arrival date gets closer.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture** worries him most, because two years leaves no time to plan before retirement.
whatWouldHelp: He wants a **clear notice period**, redundancy pay and help finding work at his age.
